entry.title: Ethics and Echos
entry.content:
We’ve been here before.

With the recent issues around the Navier-Stokes problem, it has never been clearer to me that we need regulation around the development and use of superscale AI, and we need it yesterday.

My background is physics. My professors at the university I attended were largely of an older-school, experimental physicist lean. Many of them were half-traumatized by their advisors, and many of their professors were fully-traumatized by WWII. Science was quite literally weaponized, and many of the contributors faced life-long struggles with the ethics and outcomes of their choices and works.

My undergrad training was filled with hardcore math, some entry experimentalism (see: undergrad), and a lot — like very much a lot — of ethics in science. There was a palpable ethos in our courses, lectures, seminars, and even in the offhand comments of our professors: “make sure you can live with the down-stream results of anything you choose to work on”.

I’ve always taken it seriously, so much so that I’ve taken it for granted. I thought all branches of science were as aware of the need to responsibly consider the outcomes of their research.

I was, in two words, unbelievably wrong. Or maybe naive. Probably both.

My excellent professors at one tiny, excellent, private university did not represent a real slice of scientific ethics, and especially not cross-field. And then I went and crossed fields, and I was simply not prepared for how different a world it is out here.

Computer science as a machine has not really slowed, at any point, long enough to consider the ethics of their products. Our products. Sometimes, there are mutterings about ethics, or murmurations about policy, but so often, the need for responsibility and care is shooed and scorned under the ever-mounting pressure of harder, better, faster, more, more, more.

Here’s an example.

How often in CS or tech are we hearing:
“if we don’t do it first, someone else will, so it might as well be us”?

Now where have we heard that before?

I’m not arguing for cessation. If AI is here, then it is here, and the new arms race is underway. But like the last go-around, this field needs safeguards, regulation, care, consideration, and above-all a purpose, and one that is outside profit margins. I’m certainly not saying the government can be expected to always make the best, most ethical choices with a touchy branch of research. But I am saying “move fast and break things” should emphatically not apply to superscale AI.

The idea of letting the characterized amoral tech-bro sell nuclear bombs to whomever can afford it is the literal premise of many a kitsch novel and movie. Look at the messes with social media — do we want those same morals in control of this generation’s atomic weapon? No? Because that is what we are doing. We are simply playing with fire and hoping the house doesn’t burn down.

We’ve been here before. We arguably got lucky that the world is in one piece after the last time around, and we were being orders of magnitude more cautious back then.

We can and must do this better.

Photograph (of J. Robert Oppenheimer) taken from the very excellent 1965 NBC News televised discussion of the trinity test and Manhattan project: The decision to drop the bomb. NBC-TV, executive producer : Irving Gitlin, 1965.
entry.summary: We find ourselves on familiar and unsettling grounds.

entry.title: K and R - The C Answer Book

link.title: K and R - The C Answer Book

entry.content:
The C Programming Language

by Kernighan and Ritchie

Reviewed September 2023

This book:
  • Stands the test of time
  • Respects the reader
  • while still being approachable
  • Has examples, examples, and more examples
Expected read-time is 10-20 hours -- it really depends on your experience and comfort with C.

Disclaimer

Please remember this book was published in 1988!

It’s absolutely fabulous as an intro. Some of the advanced topics are out of date, however, and some of the practices are outdated.

An example is putting all variable declarations at the top of a file - this is now an anti-pattern as it ineffectively uses memory. It had a place in the past, but no longer. Another example is declaring variables in if/else-if statements - this is also not recommended, as it causes unexpected side-effects and can be hard to read. A better method is to define variables as-needed around if/else-if statements and use the variables. Exceptions, of course, are made for loop-contained variables, especially indices and similar in for/while loops. In general though, don’t have your code have side-effects!

The K&R was written by the people who designed and wrote C. These people are legends! And their insight into their language is amazing. So do read the book! But remember - it’s not the end-all.

That said, here’s a short reading guide:

Chapters 1, 2, 3, and 4

are your basics of C. Syntax, types, loops, functions, and basic compilation - you’ll do a hello-world here, for example.

Pitfall topics:

  • Variables and scope are easy mess up in C, and the resulting errors can be a hassle to identify.

  • Keep in mind your use of static – and how it differs if it’s inside a block vs applied to a declaration or global!

  • Dig around in the compilation process – take a look at the results of preprocessing (gcc -E), at the object dump from your assembling (gcc -c, then objdump -d file.o), and at the object dump from your linked executable.

Chapter 5

is pointers! Grab your towel and Don’t Panic. This is a well-paced walkthrough, give it a slow and purposeful read.

Pitfall topics:

  • are just what you’d expect – pointers are easy to mess up and hard to debug.

  • Remember – &variable gives you the address, *variable gives you the value at a pointer, and * in a declaration indicates a pointer.

  • C is pass-by-value! So everything is pointers - or pointers-to-pointers, even.

  • Array notation and pointer notation are mostly interchangeable – and as long as the compiler is made aware of the type the pointer references, adding to a pointer will move sizeof() !

Chapter 6

is structures - in the age of object-oriented-everything, structs should be pretty conceptually comfy.

Pitfall topics:

  • Self-referential structs require careful malloc/free – the compiler can’t be expected to know how large an object is when it contains itself, after all!

Chapter 7 and 8

cover I/O and UNIX system interfacing. These chapters are very useful but often outdated – not usually incorrect, but there are many modern developments that ease the more tricky topics in these chapters. That said, do read them, as they cover the extreme-basics. The examples in chapter 8 are especially informative. Set aside time to walk through these - maybe even try running them yourself, they’re that decent.

Remaining contents

are appendices including libraries and references manuals. I find these chapters are a good skim - but I have trouble remembering these hyper-detailed tidbits out of context/use. I did enjoy skimming, though - some of the referenced materials are weird! Especially some of the more esotheric operators.

Additionally, the Standard Library appendix does have some useful tables for printf/scanf formatting options. These are always nice to have handy to flip open.
entry.summary: The K and R book is awesome - I've reread it to teach a course!
